strengths: The study has unusually broad empirical coverage: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 160 questions across 16 categories, and eight defenses, supplemented by transferability, efficiency, token-length, and longitudinal analyses. Review based on the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1xcnz_if/call-b1c14689e3474926b5fa613d425d2dd4/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The taxonomy and unified-policy framing organize a fragmented literature and expose meaningful model-, attack-, and category-level variation rather than reporting only a single aggregate success rate.

The response judge receives useful validation: 640 responses, three annotators, Krippendorff's alpha of 0.87, and 94.84% agreement with majority-vote human labels. This is substantially better evidence than using an unvalidated LLM judge.
The topic is highly relevant to NLP safety, and the extensive appendices, fine-grained tables, explicit limitations, and ethical discussion make the intended contribution generally understandable.
weaknesses: The evaluation conflates jailbreak success with compliance against the union of five providers' policies, even when a tested model is not governed by a given policy. Several categories already have baseline ASRs of 0.79-0.94. Consequently, raw ASR can measure ordinary policy mismatch rather than an attack-induced safety failure. Provider-matched results, attack lift conditional on baseline refusal, and response harmfulness/severity are needed to support the central risk claims.

Attack comparisons are not resource-matched. A 'step' can mean different numbers of target, attacker, and evaluator calls; GCG/COLD receive 500 optimization steps, GE succeeds if any of 50 generations works, and fixed-template methods have another regime. Some methods are evaluated on only five open models, yet averages are juxtaposed with nine-model averages. The claim that LAA is best is therefore not established under a common threat model or budget.

The implementations are not consistently faithful. Most notably, the reported MasterKey condition replaces the unavailable fine-tuned system with GPT-4 rewriting AIM using one published template, so it is not an evaluation of the claimed fine-tuning-based attack. COLD also uses a substitute setting because the intended configurations were unavailable.

The defense conclusions lack benign-prompt false-positive rates, utility measurements, calibration at common operating points, and adaptive attacks that optimize against the defended pipeline. The order and decision rule for composing all eight defenses are unspecified. A cascade can obtain near-zero ASR simply by overblocking, so the results do not establish practical defense effectiveness. The asserted explanation based on prompt diversity is also not measured directly.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings: there is no artifact link for code, the 160 questions, generated prompts, outputs, or labels; the judge's influential few-shot demonstrations are omitted; attack repository commits and random seeds are absent; and mutable API aliases and main-experiment dates are insufficiently specified.

Statistical support is limited. Category-level results use only ten questions, stochastic attacks apparently have no documented repeated runs, and no confidence intervals, paired tests, or sensitivity analyses are reported. Judge validation lacks class balance, confusion matrices, and multilingual/obfuscation-specific accuracy, while its permissive 'any relevant content or willingness' criterion may count non-actionable responses.

These are central soundness and reproducibility concerns rather than reservations about subjective interest. The breadth is promising, but policy-matched evaluation, fair budgets, faithful implementations, utility-aware defenses, uncertainty estimates, and a complete artifact require important revision before a Findings recommendation.

strengths: The study is highly relevant to NLP safety and unusually broad: it evaluates 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 160 questions spanning 16 categories, and eight defenses, alongside transferability, efficiency, and longitudinal analyses. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-oai5pz79/call-0c4fca9d179c45d5b954d32606bc77d6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The taxonomy and accompanying comparison of access requirements, question modification, and seed dependence provide a useful organizational view of a fragmented literature.

The authors make a serious effort to validate automatic evaluation: 640 responses are independently annotated by three annotators, with reported Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% agreement between the proposed judge and majority labels.
The paper is generally clear and supplies extensive fine-grained results, attack configurations, policy definitions, limitations, and ethical discussion.
weaknesses: The central construct is insufficiently valid. Questions are declared violations independently of the generated answer, and the union of providers’ usage policies is applied even to models whose providers do not prohibit a category. Moreover, the judge primarily tests whether a response is relevant or shows willingness to comply, not whether it supplies substantively harmful or policy-violating information. Human agreement with this labeling rule does not establish that it measures actual jailbreak harm. The very high baseline rates in several categories make this concern consequential.

Attack comparisons do not use equivalent budgets. Most methods are evaluated from one selected response, whereas Generation Exploitation succeeds if any of 50 generations succeeds. The proposed notion of a “step” also does not equalize target-model queries, candidate evaluations, auxiliary-model calls, or computation. In addition, averages compare methods tested on nine models with white-box methods tested on only five. Consequently, rankings such as LAA or GE being strongest/most efficient are not supported as fair comparisons.

The headline explanation that seed-based prompts lack diversity and therefore fail under defenses is not directly tested: no lexical, semantic, or distributional diversity measurement is reported. Defense evaluation also omits benign false-positive rates, utility degradation, latency/cost, adaptive attacks, and sufficient details about the ordering/configuration of the eight-defense composition. Near-zero ASR could therefore reflect an impractically aggressive filter rather than a useful defense.

Statistical support is weak. Category-level conclusions often rest on only ten questions, yet there are no repeated stochastic runs, random-seed specifications, confidence intervals, or significance analyses. Longitudinal changes are attributed to undocumented model updates without controls that separate updates from sampling or service variation.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings: the manuscript provides no release link for its code, 160-question dataset, outputs, or annotations; the three judge demonstrations are explicitly omitted; the question-generation model and detailed provenance are unspecified; mutable API aliases and main evaluation dates are missing; and implementation commits and several defense thresholds are not given. MasterKey is represented by a template-based reimplementation, while COLD uses a modified setting because the repository was incomplete, further weakening comparability.

The taxonomy’s boundaries are partly subjective and overlapping, and some categories contain only one or two methods. Category-level recommendations—especially deprioritizing heuristic attacks—are therefore broader than the evidence supports. Overall, the experimental scale is promising, but correcting the outcome definition, normalizing budgets, and releasing sufficient artifacts are important revisions before the benchmark can support a sound, reproducible Findings contribution.

strengths: The empirical scope is unusually broad: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 160 questions across 16 policy categories, eight defenses, and supplementary transferability, efficiency, prompt-length, and longitudinal analyses. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-j8j4ioq2/call-29f0cfbdd93d40a899ee4c1c3434421d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The paper makes a serious standardization effort and reports model settings, compute resources, attack hyperparameters, access assumptions, and detailed method-level results rather than only headline averages.

The automatic evaluator receives meaningful human validation: 640 sampled outputs, three annotators, Krippendorff's alpha of 0.87, and 94.84% agreement with majority labels, substantially exceeding the reported alternative evaluators.

The observed variation across attacks and defenses is practically useful. In particular, the sharp degradation of known seed/template attacks under several filters, contrasted with the residual success of DrAttack, PAIR, and TAP, motivates useful follow-up work.
weaknesses: The central construct is not consistently a jailbreak. The union of five vendors' policies is applied to every target, including models from other providers, although many categories are not prohibited by each target's own policy. Baseline ASR is 0.78-0.94 for six categories, so pooled ASRs and model rankings often measure ordinary compliance rather than bypassing a safeguard. Results should be conditioned on target-specific policies and compared as attack-induced uplift over the direct-query baseline.

The judge primarily measures relevance or non-refusal: its prompt explicitly says to ignore legality and ethics and accepts any relevant indirect content. It does not establish that an answer is harmful, actionable, correct, or actually policy-violating. Human agreement supports reliability under this definition, not its construct validity; moreover, aggregate judge error is not stratified by attack, category, language, or model.

Attack comparisons are not demonstrably budget-matched. A 'step' can represent very different numbers of target queries, candidates, auxiliary-model calls, tokens, and compute; GCG/COLD receive 500 steps, GE is successful if any of 50 generations works, and applicability differs between local and API models. Altered implementations of COLD and especially MasterKey further weaken method rankings.

The taxonomy mixes non-orthogonal dimensions: surface transformation, search algorithm, training procedure, and decoding access. Heuristic optimization also uses feedback, and methods can naturally occupy multiple categories. More importantly, the claimed causal explanation that seed-based prompts are less diverse or natural is never measured or isolated; defense outcomes alone do not establish it.

The defense study reports no benign-input pass rate, false-positive rate, or utility cost, and does not adequately specify guard placement, thresholds, ordering, or the eight-defense composition. A reject-everything cascade would obtain excellent ASR, so these results cannot support claims about practical defense effectiveness or attack practicality.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a benchmark contribution: the 160 questions, generated prompts, outputs, and implementation are not released or linked; the judge demonstrations are omitted; the question-generation model and detailed selection provenance are unspecified; and random seeds, repeated stochastic runs, confidence intervals, exact API measurement dates/snapshots, and output-length settings are missing.

The novelty positioning does not engage with major contemporary standardized resources such as HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and StrongREJECT. This weakens the claims of being the first or most comprehensive benchmark and leaves the chosen dataset and evaluator insufficiently calibrated against current alternatives. Overall, the breadth makes the paper promising, but these soundness and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The manuscript undertakes an unusually broad and highly relevant empirical study: 17 attacks, nine open- and closed-weight LLMs, 160 questions spanning 16 categories, and eight defenses. This scale could make the study useful to the NLP-safety community. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-qqlyu0b0/call-539f35595fc54fdeac286dbc083b2373/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation extends beyond a single ASR table: direct and transfer attacks, longitudinal measurements, runtime, prompt length, policy-category breakdowns, and defenses provide several complementary views of the attack landscape.

The authors make a serious attempt to improve automatic evaluation. Their GPT-4 judge is compared with 640 triply annotated responses, obtaining Krippendorff's alpha of 0.87 among annotators and 94.84% agreement with majority labels, substantially above the reported alternative evaluators.

The taxonomy and consolidated configuration tables offer useful organizational value, while the paper clearly discusses limitations, computational resources, ethics, and several implementation deviations.
weaknesses: The central construct is not cleanly a jailbreak. The union of five providers' policies is applied to every model even though Table 9 shows that many categories are not prohibited by every provider. Consequently, compliant answers to an out-of-scope policy may be counted as attacks; baseline ASRs reach 0.94 for AI Usage Disclosure and exceed attack ASRs in several categories. Provider-conditioned results and attack-induced uplift over the direct-query baseline are needed before claims about bypassing safeguards are valid.

The judge validation establishes consistency with the authors' labels, but not construct validity. The success rule effectively accepts any relevant, non-rephrasing information and does not require the response to be harmful, correct, actionable, or materially more useful to an attacker; Table 14 even labels unspecified 'general advice' as success. This weakens conclusions about real harmful capability.

Comparisons are not adequately controlled. Fixed one-query templates, methods allowed up to 50 modifications or responses, and gradient methods given 500 optimization steps do not receive comparable target-query or compute budgets. MasterKey is not actually reproduced, COLD uses a substitute configuration because the repository is incomplete, and LAA sometimes uses another model's configuration. Moreover, model averages are computed over different attack subsets because several methods cannot target closed models, making cross-model vulnerability rankings confounded.

The defense conclusions lack essential controls: no benign-prompt false-positive rate, utility retention, latency, or cost is reported; the exact ordering/composition of the eight-defense stack is unclear; and it is not established that attacks adapt to deployed defenses. Thus, near-zero ASR could reflect indiscriminate rejection, and the claims that seed-based attacks are impractical or easy to mitigate are not supported. Prompt diversity and naturalness—the proposed causal explanation—are never quantitatively measured.

Only ten questions represent each category, yet no confidence intervals, repeated trials, sensitivity analyses, or significance tests are provided. Numerous causal interpretations—about training data, provider priorities, hidden model updates, seed dependence, and enhanced category-specific guardrails—are plausible hypotheses rather than findings isolated by the experiments.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for Findings: the manuscript provides no artifact link; the 160-question dataset, generated prompts, model responses, human labels, and harmful few-shot judge demonstrations are unavailable; and random seeds, complete decoding limits, software revisions, main-experiment dates, and exact proprietary model snapshots are missing. Mutable APIs further magnify these omissions.

The claimed novelty and comprehensiveness are insufficiently established. The taxonomy mixes overlapping axes such as prompt origin, optimization procedure, training, and decoding access, while selecting 17 of more than 200 attacks primarily by citation count. Comparison with prominent contemporary jailbreak benchmarks and stronger harmfulness evaluators is also incomplete. Overall, the breadth is promising, but these soundness and reproducibility concerns keep the paper just below a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP-safety problem through an unusually broad empirical study: 17 attacks, nine target LLMs, 160 questions across 16 categories, and eight defenses, supplemented by transferability, runtime, prompt-length, and longitudinal analyses.

The extensive per-method, per-model, and per-category results could become a valuable benchmark resource. The paper also reports attack access requirements, applicability limitations, several hyperparameters, and compute specifications.

The automatic judge receives meaningful human validation: 640 sampled responses were independently annotated by three annotators, with Krippendorff's alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% agreement with the resulting human labels. This is substantially stronger than relying only on refusal-string matching.
The manuscript is relevant to ACL, generally well organized, and appropriately acknowledges limitations of automated jailbreak evaluation and temporally changing APIs.
weaknesses: The central measurement conflates safeguard bypass with policy noncompliance. A union of five providers' policies is applied to every model even where Table 9 marks a category as absent, and several categories concern downstream use or context rather than content that a model must categorically refuse. Baseline ASRs reach 0.78–0.94 in six categories, while the judge counts any relevant information or willingness and explicitly does not assess harmfulness or response quality. Consequently, many reported successes need not represent jailbreaks, weakening claims about model vulnerability and access to harmful resources.

The attack comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Methods are evaluated on different target sets, under different access assumptions, and with incomparable budgets: 50 modification steps, 500 GCG/COLD steps, unequal auxiliary and target-model calls, and success over any of 50 generation settings for GE. Model-specific LAA templates and an approximate MasterKey reimplementation add further asymmetry. Averages therefore combine different method and model sets, confounding headline rankings such as LAA being best or DeepSeek-V3 being most vulnerable.

The taxonomy mixes orthogonal properties and is not clearly mutually exclusive: heuristic search also receives evaluation feedback, while fine-tuning describes an implementation mechanism rather than prompt behavior. More importantly, claims that seed use causes low diversity and detectability, that feedback-based prompts are more natural and diverse, and that heuristic attacks have low practicality are not supported by direct diversity, naturalness, distributional, or causal analyses. They are inferred from only one to four selected methods per category.

The defense study is under-specified and insufficient for practical conclusions. It does not clearly document input-versus-output filtering, thresholds, the order and logic used to compose all eight defenses, or whether attacks adapt to deployed defenses. It also omits benign false-positive rates and utility costs, and some defenses do not cover all 16 policy categories. Thus low ASR alone cannot establish that a defense is effective or practical.

Statistical reliability is limited. There are only ten questions per category, apparently one stochastic run per condition, no random seeds, repeated trials, uncertainty intervals, paired tests, or sensitivity analyses. The 640-example judge validation lacks class balance, stratification, confusion statistics, and uncertainty. Longitudinal changes are attributed to undocumented model updates without accounting for API nondeterminism or providing error bars.

Reproducibility falls below the Findings bar. The manuscript provides no code or dataset repository; the 160 questions, generated prompts, responses, annotations, and judge demonstrations are unavailable. The question-generation model is unspecified, exact API snapshots and main-experiment dates are missing, and several chat templates, output limits, seeds, defense configurations, and thresholds are not reported. Omitting the judge's few-shot examples also prevents reconstruction of the principal outcome measure. These omissions are particularly consequential for a paper presented as a reusable benchmark.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important, ACL-relevant LLM-safety problem with unusually broad empirical coverage: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 16 policy categories, eight defenses, transferability, efficiency, and longitudinal behavior. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rzsbi8k9/call-2930974c98d74c94b5455914bfa6ef26/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The taxonomy and unified-policy framework provide a useful organizing view of a fragmented literature, while the numerous fine-grained result matrices could be valuable to practitioners.

The automatic evaluator receives meaningful validation: 640 randomly selected responses, three annotators, Krippendorff's alpha of 0.87, and 94.84% agreement with majority human labels, substantially above the reported baselines.
The paper reports model and hardware information, attack hyperparameters, direct and transfer baselines, and candid limitations and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: The main ASR has serious construct-validity problems. The union of five providers' policies is applied to every model even when the model's provider does not prohibit a category. Moreover, the judge tests whether a response addresses the request rather than whether it materially violates the target's policy or causes harm. With an overall no-attack baseline of 0.42 and category baselines reaching 0.94, many counted successes are not demonstrated safeguard bypasses. Results should be policy-conditioned and report attack uplift or success among prompts refused at baseline.

Attack rankings are not based on comparable budgets. GE receives 50 decoding configurations and succeeds if any response passes, whereas other methods are reported as top-1; iterative budgets range from 50 modifications to 500 GCG/COLD steps; auxiliary-query costs and access assumptions differ; and averages compare methods evaluated on five models with methods evaluated on nine. No repeated random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests quantify stochastic variability.

The central explanation that seed-based prompts lack diversity and are therefore impractical under defenses is not established experimentally. Prompt diversity and naturalness are never measured or controlled, attacks are not adaptively optimized against the defenses, and PromptGuard may simply recognize known templates. Defense results also omit clean-input false-positive rates and utility, so a filter or eight-defense ensemble could appear effective by overblocking.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a claimed benchmark tool: there is no release link for the 160 questions, outputs, labels, or evaluation code; essential few-shot judge demonstrations are omitted; and repository commits, random seeds, main experiment dates, and stable proprietary-model snapshots are absent. MasterKey is replaced by a GPT-4 rewrite of AIM rather than its fine-tuning procedure, while COLD uses an altered configuration because the public implementation was incomplete.

The proposed taxonomy mixes non-exclusive axes—heuristic methods also consume optimization feedback, while fine-tuning describes model construction rather than prompt-generation behavior—and the evaluated MasterKey proxy does not fit its assigned category. Transferability is tested from only Vicuna, and citation-based attack selection plus several dated models weakens the claim of comprehensiveness. Collectively, these concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation, though the study's scale makes the case borderline rather than fundamentally unsalvageable.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP-safety problem with unusually broad empirical scope: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 16 violation categories, eight defenses, and direct, transfer, longitudinal, efficiency, and prompt-length analyses. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-20_f6mxy/call-3f543c3d29c04067ac0280bb5f76b251/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The response evaluator is more carefully validated than the common substring and single-label baselines: 640 responses receive three independent human annotations, with Krippendorff's alpha of 0.87 and reported agreement of 94.84% with the proposed judge.
The paper makes a serious effort to harmonize attack budgets and documents access assumptions, principal hyperparameters, compute, attack applicability, and baseline results.
The extensive per-model and per-category results, transfer experiments, and longitudinal measurements could become a useful empirical resource.
The observed contrast between seed-based attacks and attacks such as PAIR or TAP under prompt filters is practically interesting, although the causal explanation requires stronger validation.
weaknesses: The central evaluation conflates policy violation with jailbreak effectiveness. A union of five providers' policies is applied to models from other providers and to categories that a given provider may not prohibit. Baseline ASRs reach 0.94 for AI Usage Disclosure and 0.86 for Political Activities, and attacks often reduce rather than increase compliance. Raw ASR therefore does not isolate attack-induced safeguard bypass; provider-aligned policies and a paired refusal-to-harmful-compliance or attack-lift metric are needed.

The success criterion counts any relevant information or willingness as a successful jailbreak without assessing harmfulness, actionability, or response quality. Judge validation reports only aggregate accuracy, without class prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, or stratification by model, category, language, and obfuscation type; its roughly 5% disagreement is also larger than many reported differences.

Comparisons are not adequately controlled. GE receives 50 generation settings and succeeds if any response passes, while most methods report a top-1 outcome; GCG and COLD receive 500 optimization steps versus 50 modifications elsewhere; and averages mix methods applicable to five models with methods applicable to nine. Randomized attacks appear to have only one run, with no seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or robustness analysis despite only ten questions per category.

The defense conclusions omit benign utility and false-positive rates, so low ASR alone cannot establish an effective or practical defense. The order and decision rule for composing all eight defenses, policy mappings and thresholds, and input-versus-output filtering are insufficiently specified. Prompt diversity and naturalness are asserted rather than measured, making the proposed causal explanation about initial seeds speculative.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a benchmark contribution. The manuscript provides no artifact containing its exact question set, responses, or evaluation code; does not identify the dataset-generation model; and omits the judge's few-shot demonstrations. It also approximates MasterKey because its code is unavailable, uses incomplete COLD settings, lacks random seeds and complete chat-template details, and relies partly on mutable API systems without clearly dated primary runs.

The proposed taxonomy is not clearly mutually exclusive or consistently defined: heuristic methods also consume optimization feedback, while fine-tuning describes how an attacker model is trained rather than the mechanism of the resulting jailbreak. The empirically important seed/no-seed distinction is merely an auxiliary attribute rather than a taxonomy axis.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence, including claims about providers' safety priorities, internal detection rules, safety-training trade-offs, and semantic causes of transfer. The breadth and practical interest are substantial, but they do not compensate for the validity and reproducibility gaps; important revisions are needed before the work meets the Findings threshold.

strengths: Substantial and relevant empirical scope: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 160 questions, eight defenses, and additional transfer, efficiency, prompt-length, and longitudinal analyses.
The authors attempt to standardize evaluation and document model identifiers, hardware, attack hyperparameters, and judging instructions in extensive appendices.

The GPT-4 judge is checked against 640 responses labeled by three annotators, with reported Krippendorff's alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% agreement with majority labels—considerably better than the evaluated alternatives.
Direct-query baselines and per-model/per-category results expose meaningful heterogeneity that could support a useful benchmark after methodological revision.
The paper is organized, readable, and clearly relevant to NLP and LLM safety.
weaknesses: The central ASR construct does not reliably identify jailbreaks. The dataset unions policies from five providers and applies every category to every model, including models whose providers do not prohibit that category and rules governing downstream use rather than model output. Several categories have baseline ASRs of 0.78-0.94, yet raw compliance is still called jailbreak success instead of measuring paired success on requests initially refused or attack-induced uplift.

The cross-method comparison is not fair despite that being a central claim. Methods receive different opportunity budgets: 50 prompt modifications, 500 GCG/COLD steps, or best-of-50 generations for Generation Exploitation. Some averages cover five open models while others cover nine models, but the methods are ranked together. Query-, token-, and compute-matched curves are needed.

Implementation fidelity is questionable. MasterKey is replaced with an AIM rewrite because its code is unavailable; COLD uses only one setting because the repository is reportedly incorrect; and LAA reuses a Llama-3 configuration for unsupported targets. These variants are not validated against reference results.

The defense study omits benign rejection rates and utility tradeoffs. It also does not adequately specify the ordering and decision rule for combining eight heterogeneous defenses or whether attacks adapt to the defended pipeline. Thus, near-zero ASR may reflect indiscriminate filtering rather than a practical defense.

Statistical rigor is insufficient: no random seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance analyses are reported. Category claims rely on only ten questions each. Fine-grained cells occurring in increments such as 0.03 and 0.07 are also inconsistent with the stated ten-question, single-response protocol unless an undisclosed replication scheme was used.

The proposed taxonomy mixes non-exclusive dimensions—prompt provenance, obfuscation, optimization, training procedure, and decoding intervention—and contains only one to four heterogeneous attacks per category. Claims that seed use or taxonomy membership explains defense robustness are correlational; prompt diversity is neither quantified nor causally ablated.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript supplies no release link for the new dataset, prompts, responses, labels, code, or adapted implementations. The question-generating model, repository commits, random seeds, main-experiment query dates, and harmful few-shot judge examples are missing, while several results depend on mutable proprietary APIs.

Judge validation reports only aggregate agreement without class prevalence, confusion matrices, or subgroup performance. Its definition counts any relevant information or willingness as success without assessing correctness, harmfulness, or actionability, so claims about misuse severity, fully effective attacks, and developers' safety priorities exceed the evidence. Important reanalysis and budget-matched, utility-aware experiments are needed before the work is suitable for Findings.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for ACL 2025, using the ACL Rolling Review overall-assessment criteria.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess the validity of the central claims, the suitability and rigor of the methodology, the adequacy of supporting evidence, reproducibility, clarity, and relevance to computational linguistics and natural language processing. Evaluate the contribution in light of its stated aims. Distinguish evidence of soundness from subjective interest, novelty, and prospective impact.

A sound Findings recommendation need not imply that the paper has a technical defect. Do not compute the overall assessment by averaging separate dimensions or treating personal excitement as a substitute for evidence. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, or 5.

Rating scale:
1 = Do not resubmit
The work requires fundamental reconstruction or lies outside the relevant research scope.

1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle
Substantial work is required, on a timescale longer than the next review cycle.

2 = Resubmit next cycle
Important revisions remain, but a revised submission could reasonably be ready for the next cycle.

The case for Findings is close, with unresolved concerns preventing a clear positive recommendation.

3 = Findings
The paper supports a sound and reproducible contribution suitable for Findings.

3.5 = Borderline Conference
The main-conference recommendation is close; explain what limits confidence in that recommendation.

4 = Conference
The paper warrants main-conference publication based on its supported contribution and overall merits.

The paper is a plausible outstanding-paper candidate, with reservations about that distinction.

This breadth makes otherwise difficult cross-method and cross-model comparisons possible.","The evaluation extends beyond aggregate attack success rates to transferability, runtime, prompt length, longitudinal behavior, policy categories, and defenses. The observed contrast between recognizable seed-based attacks and more diverse attacks is potentially actionable.","The response judge is evaluated against 640 responses labeled by three annotators, with Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% agreement. This is appreciably stronger validation than relying uncritically on string matching or an unvalidated LLM judge.","The manuscript is clearly organized and unusually transparent about many implementation details, including model identifiers, attack budgets, hardware, defense configurations, category definitions, and limitations. The extensive tables and appendices make the descriptive results accessible."],"weaknesses":["The central construct is not cleanly a jailbreak measure. Direct prompting already has a mean ASR of 0.42, reaching 0.78–0.94 in several categories, while the unified policy includes prohibitions that do not apply to every evaluated provider or model. Because attack success is neither conditioned on baseline refusal nor reported as uplift over baseline, claims about bypassing safeguards and model vulnerability conflate genuine jailbreaks, pre-existing noncompliance, and disagreement with an externally imposed policy.","The claimed unified, fair comparison uses materially different evaluation conditions. Some attacks are evaluated on only five open models while others use all nine; 50 prompt-modification steps, 500 gradient steps, fixed templates, and GE’s best-of-50 criterion are not comparable budgets. MasterKey is approximated without its original implementation, and COLD uses a restricted configuration because the repository is incomplete. Paired comparisons, normalized query/compute budgets, repeated runs, and uncertainty estimates are needed before declaring one family or attack superior.","The proposed taxonomy mixes overlapping dimensions such as prompt provenance, optimization algorithm, feedback signal, training requirements, and decoding access. Heuristic methods such as genetic search and mutation also consume evaluation feedback, while feedback-based methods also perform heuristic search. Consequently, the conclusion that heuristic methods are intrinsically less robust is confounded with seed dependence and is generalized from only a few selected attacks without a controlled seed/diversity ablation.","The defense study lacks benign-input false-positive rates, utility retention, adaptive attackers, and clear details about the order and thresholds used when composing all defenses. A filter that rejects every input would obtain zero ASR under the reported evaluation. Generation Exploitation is also absent from the defense table. Thus, the results support effectiveness against these static attack instances, not the broader claims about practical mitigation.","The judge validation reports aggregate agreement without class-specific precision/recall, confidence intervals, or clearly stratified sampling across attacks, models, categories, and defenses. GPT-4 also participates in generating or optimizing several attacks and serves as the final judge, creating possible evaluator coupling. With only ten questions per category and no repeated stochastic trials, many fine-grained differences are not statistically supported.","Reproducibility is presently inadequate for the paper’s benchmark claim. There is no stated artifact link; the exact 160 questions, generated outputs, dataset-construction model and source proportions, repository commits, random seeds, and exact defense composition are unavailable. strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP-safety problem at substantial scale: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 160 questions across 16 policy categories, and eight defenses. This breadth makes otherwise difficult cross-method and cross-model comparisons possible.

The evaluation extends beyond aggregate attack success rates to transferability, runtime, prompt length, longitudinal behavior, policy categories, and defenses. The observed contrast between recognizable seed-based attacks and more diverse attacks is potentially actionable.

The response judge is evaluated against 640 responses labeled by three annotators, with Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% agreement. This is appreciably stronger validation than relying uncritically on string matching or an unvalidated LLM judge.

The manuscript is clearly organized and unusually transparent about many implementation details, including model identifiers, attack budgets, hardware, defense configurations, category definitions, and limitations. The extensive tables and appendices make the descriptive results accessible.
weaknesses: The central construct is not cleanly a jailbreak measure. Direct prompting already has a mean ASR of 0.42, reaching 0.78–0.94 in several categories, while the unified policy includes prohibitions that do not apply to every evaluated provider or model. Because attack success is neither conditioned on baseline refusal nor reported as uplift over baseline, claims about bypassing safeguards and model vulnerability conflate genuine jailbreaks, pre-existing noncompliance, and disagreement with an externally imposed policy.

The claimed unified, fair comparison uses materially different evaluation conditions. Some attacks are evaluated on only five open models while others use all nine; 50 prompt-modification steps, 500 gradient steps, fixed templates, and GE’s best-of-50 criterion are not comparable budgets. MasterKey is approximated without its original implementation, and COLD uses a restricted configuration because the repository is incomplete. Paired comparisons, normalized query/compute budgets, repeated runs, and uncertainty estimates are needed before declaring one family or attack superior.

The proposed taxonomy mixes overlapping dimensions such as prompt provenance, optimization algorithm, feedback signal, training requirements, and decoding access. Heuristic methods such as genetic search and mutation also consume evaluation feedback, while feedback-based methods also perform heuristic search. Consequently, the conclusion that heuristic methods are intrinsically less robust is confounded with seed dependence and is generalized from only a few selected attacks without a controlled seed/diversity ablation.

The defense study lacks benign-input false-positive rates, utility retention, adaptive attackers, and clear details about the order and thresholds used when composing all defenses. A filter that rejects every input would obtain zero ASR under the reported evaluation. Generation Exploitation is also absent from the defense table. Thus, the results support effectiveness against these static attack instances, not the broader claims about practical mitigation.

The judge validation reports aggregate agreement without class-specific precision/recall, confidence intervals, or clearly stratified sampling across attacks, models, categories, and defenses. GPT-4 also participates in generating or optimizing several attacks and serves as the final judge, creating possible evaluator coupling. With only ten questions per category and no repeated stochastic trials, many fine-grained differences are not statistically supported.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for the paper’s benchmark claim. There is no stated artifact link; the exact 160 questions, generated outputs, dataset-construction model and source proportions, repository commits, random seeds, and exact defense composition are unavailable. The three judge demonstrations are explicitly omitted, and several proprietary model names are mutable aliases. The dataset therefore cannot currently be reused and the reported measurements cannot be exactly replicated.

strengths: The empirical scope is unusually broad: 17 attacks, nine target models, 160 questions across 16 policy categories, eight defenses, and additional transferability, efficiency, token-length, and longitudinal analyses.

Using a shared dataset and evaluator improves comparability over isolated attack papers. Applicability constraints, hyperparameters, and several implementation deviations are documented transparently.

The three-part GPT-4 evaluator is more careful than string matching or a single-label judge. Its validation uses 640 responses, three annotators, Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87, and 94.84% agreement with majority human labels.
The paper is clearly organized, empirically informative, and highly relevant to LLM safety research in NLP.
weaknesses: The central ASR construct has questionable validity. A response can count as successful when it provides any relevant information, willingness, or effective general advice; harmfulness, actionability, correctness, and actual policy violation are not directly assessed. Human agreement validates consistency with this definition, not the definition itself, and no class balance, confusion matrix, or category-wise judge accuracy is reported.

The union of five providers’ policies is applied across models governed by different policies, including models from other providers. Broad or deployment-level categories such as AI Usage Disclosure, Political Activities, and Unauthorized Practice do not necessarily imply that a model should refuse every associated query. Baseline ASRs as high as 0.94 suggest substantial task-policy mismatch, yet the exact 160 questions are not provided for audit.

Attack comparisons are not budget-matched: fixed-template methods may receive one query, iterative methods receive up to 50 modifications, GE is declared successful if any of 50 generations succeeds, and GCG/COLD receive 500 optimization steps. Auxiliary-model calls and target queries also differ. Moreover, row averages mix methods evaluated on five models with methods evaluated on nine, weakening rankings such as one attack being best overall.

Defense results omit benign-prompt false-positive rates and utility preservation, so near-zero ASR could reflect indiscriminate rejection rather than a practically effective defense. Composition order, several thresholds, and training-data overlap with evaluated attacks are insufficiently controlled. The claimed causal explanation based on seed dependence and prompt diversity is not directly measured or experimentally isolated.

The taxonomy mixes nonexclusive dimensions—prompt provenance, transformation mechanism, optimization procedure, training, and decoding. Heuristic methods themselves consume evaluative feedback, while fine-tuned or human-seeded methods can also use obfuscation. Consequently, broad family-level conclusions drawn from only one to four hand-selected methods per family are fragile.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings: there is no paper artifact containing the dataset, raw outputs, full judge demonstrations, attack prompts, implementation code, exact repository commits, random seeds, or complete API snapshot dates. MasterKey is approximated without its code, COLD uses a workaround because configurations are unavailable, and proprietary judges/models are mutable. No repeated stochastic runs, confidence intervals, or significance analyses are reported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, clearly NLP-relevant safety problem and assembles an unusually broad evaluation: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 160 questions across 16 policy categories, and eight defenses.

The empirical coverage extends beyond headline attack-success rates to transferability, runtime, prompt length, longitudinal behavior, and defense bypass rates. These analyses expose useful practical differences among attacks.

The response evaluator receives meaningful validation: 640 responses are independently labeled by three annotators, with Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% agreement between the proposed judge and majority human labels. This is substantially stronger than relying on refusal-string matching alone.
The paper documents many implementation choices, including model identifiers, temperature, hardware, attack hyperparameters, and deviations necessitated by unavailable or broken implementations.
The manuscript is generally well organized, presents extensive results, acknowledges several limitations, and responsibly excludes child-endangerment queries.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is construct validity. A union of five providers’ usage policies is applied to every target model, including models from other providers and categories that some evaluated providers do not explicitly prohibit. Usage policies are also not necessarily model-level refusal specifications. The resulting baseline ASR is already 0.42 overall and reaches 0.78–0.94 in several categories, indicating that the benchmark often measures whether a model answers a broadly policy-associated request rather than whether an attack bypasses an operative safeguard. This weakens cross-model safety comparisons and claims about real-world jailbreak risk.

Attack comparisons are not adequately controlled. A nominal “step” represents different numbers of target queries, candidate generations, auxiliary-model calls, and amounts of computation across methods; GCG/COLD receive 500 steps, GE is successful if any of 50 generation settings works, and other methods receive heterogeneous search procedures. Averages also compare attacks evaluated on nine models with white-box attacks evaluated on only five. Thus rankings such as “LAA performs best” and taxonomy-level comparisons are confounded by budgets and target coverage.

No repeated stochastic trials, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This is especially problematic for mutation/search attacks and for category-level results based on only ten questions per category. Small numerical differences and longitudinal fluctuations therefore cannot support the paper’s comparative or update-related interpretations.

The central explanation that seed-based attacks fail because their prompts lack diversity is asserted rather than demonstrated. The paper provides no diversity or naturalness measure, controlled seed ablation, or analysis of possible overlap with defense training data. The experiments establish an association between named attacks and detection rates, not the proposed causal mechanism.

The defense evaluation contains no benign inputs, false-positive rates, retained utility, or end-to-end cost. Consequently, near-zero ASR—especially after cascading eight defenses—does not establish a practical defense, since an indiscriminately blocking system could obtain the same result. Defense configurations and policy mappings are also underspecified, and Generation Exploitation is omitted from the defense tables without explanation.

Although aggregate judge agreement is encouraging, class balance, precision/recall, and stratified accuracy by policy, language/encoding, attack, and model are absent. The judge criteria primarily test whether an answer contains requested information, not its policy-specific harmfulness or actionability; the paper even counts generic advice as successful. This does not fully support claims about easy access to harmful resources.

Reproducibility remains below the Findings threshold: no code or data artifact is identified; the 160 questions, generated prompts, responses, human labels, and exact human-based templates are unavailable; the judge’s three demonstrations are omitted; API snapshots, experiment dates, package versions, commits, and random seeds are incomplete. MasterKey is replaced with an unvalidated approximation and COLD uses a reduced setting because the public implementation is broken.

The proposed taxonomy is descriptively useful but not cleanly defined or strongly validated: heuristic methods also use feedback, while fine-tuning and obfuscation are orthogonal properties that can coexist with other categories. Conclusions about whole categories are drawn from very few heterogeneous methods. Overall, the study is valuable and close to Findings, but the unresolved construct-validity, comparison, and reproducibility problems prevent a sound positive recommendation in its current form.
